The friction point here hits different in sports. We spend a lot of time thinking about the gap between what a coach or analyst wants to know and the three clicks it takes to find it in a database of 500 million data points. If you're pulling tactical insights from game footage at matchday minus one, the UI is the thing eating your time budget, not the data.

What's interesting about conversational interfaces in sports is that they could flatten some real pain points in team workflows. Right now knowledge lives in SOPs that nobody fully reads, custom reports that take days to brief, and tribal knowledge from veterans who've seen 10,000 hours of footage. A system that lets a performance coach or scout just ask "which of our fullbacks reads progressive passes like Trent Alexander-Arnold" without learning a query language first isn't just nice UX - it's a multiplier for how quickly insight moves from analysis to decision.

The constraint in sports AI isn't usually the model or the data anymore. It's the gap between what the system can do and whether the person using it understands what to ask. That's where something like this feels genuinely useful - less "how do I get this" and more "what should I be looking for that I don't know to ask."

How are you seeing teams respond when you remove the need to translate their questions into technical language? Does that shift what they start exploring?
